::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will find fifteen thesis-sized questions where Earth Engine gets you started but does not finish the job. Each one comes with the reason it is still open and a first experiment you can run in a week. It also says where Python has to take over.
:::

## How to use this chapter

Each topic below is a starting point, not a promise of novelty. Research moves fast, so check the literature from the last two years before you commit. Where this book's own results show a problem, the chapter is cited. Those pilot numbers are often the best argument for why a topic is open. Three areas are highlighted because few people in Indonesia work on them yet: satellite embeddings, biomass, and LiDAR.

## A starter you can run today

GEDI measures forest structure with a spaceborne laser at scattered 25 m footprints [@dubayah2020gedi]. AlphaEarth embeddings describe every 10 m pixel with 64 learned numbers [@brown2025alphaearth]. Can the second spread the first into a wall-to-wall biomass map? The starter answers in an afternoon, and shows why testing design matters.

{{< include _snippets/ch36_thesis_starter.qmd >}}

The embeddings explain about a third of the variation in GEDI biomass, and the error is close to the spread of the data. That is a thesis, not a failure. The question is what is missing: time, texture, radar, or better labels.

## Satellite embeddings

| # | Question | Why it is open | First experiment | Python needed for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How few labels does a province-scale land cover map need with embeddings? | Chapter [-@sec-embeddings] reached 0.83 agreement with 20 points per class on one delta; nobody has shown how that holds across Indonesian landscapes | repeat the learning curve in five provinces | learning curves, uncertainty |
| 2 | Can embeddings detect smallholder deforestation that global loss maps miss? | Chapter [-@sec-eudr] showed global maps confuse rubber replanting with forest loss | compare year-to-year embedding distance with Hansen loss [@hansen2013gfc] on known farms | change metrics, labels |
| 3 | Do embeddings carry information about structure, not just cover? | the starter above: R² about 0.35 for GEDI biomass | add GEDI height (RH98) and test by block | model comparison, SHAP |

## Biomass and carbon

| # | Question | Why it is open | First experiment | Python needed for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | How much of mangrove biomass error is date and position mismatch? | Chapter [-@sec-regression]: R² near 0 because 2020 predictors met plots with no survey dates [@murdiyarso2019swampbintuni] | re-match plots to imagery of their survey year | per-plot time matching |
| 5 | Can biomass maps carry an honest uncertainty? | validation of global biomass products is still inconsistent [@duncanson2019validation] | quantile or conformal intervals, checked by block | the whole method |
| 6 | Which allometry, and how wrong is the choice? | pantropical equations [@chave2014allometric] versus local ones for Indonesian mangrove and peat forest | propagate allometry choice through a map | Monte Carlo |

## LiDAR

| # | Question | Why it is open | First experiment | Python needed for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Can individual tree stems be placed under a closed tropical canopy from airborne LiDAR? | the author's GITD work found no below-crown stem signal; the recoverable loss is crown-to-stem association (right-place height r² 0.57 against 0.19 for a detector) | train 3D segmentation on TLS-labelled ALS | point-cloud deep learning |
| 8 | How far can LiDAR plots be stretched with satellite height models? | global canopy height maps [@lang2023canopy; @potapov2021canopy] still disagree in tall tropical forest | compare both against local ALS | raster and point-cloud fusion |
| 9 | How should LiDAR samples be placed for a province? | sampling designs are reviewed [@wulder2012lidar] but rarely optimised for Indonesian landscapes | simulate flight lines over embeddings | optimisation |

## Hazards

| # | Question | Why it is open | First experiment | Python needed for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | Can a landslide model trained on one earthquake map the next? | multi-event inventories exist [@ferrario2019lombok; @xu2024caslandslide]; transfer between events is rarely tested | train on Lombok 2018, test on Palu or Cianjur | patch models, transfer |
| 11 | How big is the exposure error from missing building footprints? | Chapter [-@sec-flood]: two footprint layers differed a hundredfold in one district | compare footprint layers in 20 districts | spatial joins at scale |
| 12 | Can radar coherence warn of slope failure? | coherence needs SLC phase, which Earth Engine does not hold | coherence time series before known landslides | InSAR processing |

## Methods that change every result above

| # | Question | Why it is open | First experiment | Python needed for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | How much do published Indonesian accuracies drop under spatial validation? | random splits flatter models [@ploton2020spatial; @roberts2017cv]; Chapter [-@sec-sampling] found folds scoring up to 0.35 below a random split | re-run ten published workflows with block CV | reproducible harness |
| 14 | Where is a model allowed to predict? | area of applicability [@meyer2021aoa] is almost never mapped next to a result | add an applicability mask to Chapter [-@sec-supervised]'s map | distance in feature space |
| 15 | Are LST trends in the tropics real or orbital? | Chapter [-@sec-statistics] found broad "cooling" that may come from Terra's drifting overpass | compare Terra, Aqua and Landsat trends | cross-sensor harmonisation |

## A starter for every topic

Each topic above now has a first experiment you can run, with its real result. None of them is a thesis. Each one shows that the question is real, and gives you the first number to beat. Some results surprised us, which is the point.

### Embeddings and biomass (T1, T2, T4, T5, T6)

{{< include _snippets/ch36b_bank_carbon.qmd >}}

What they say:

- **T1.** Trained near Bandung and tested near Garut, agreement with WorldCover rises from about 0.59 with 5 labels per class to 0.73 with 100, and most of the gain comes by 10 to 20 labels. Where the curve flattens in other provinces, and against real field labels, is the open question.
- **T2.** 73 % of the pixels Hansen marks as lost in 2021 show embedding change above the 95th percentile of stable forest. The other 27 %, and the 5 % of "stable" forest that changed as much, are where smallholder loss may be hiding.
- **T4.** The correlation between Landsat NDVI and plot biomass moves between 0.05 and 0.26 depending only on the year of the image. Without survey dates, the predictor year is a hidden choice.
- **T5.** Conformal intervals calibrated on one spatial block cover only 62 % (target 80 %) and 77 % (target 90 %) of footprints on another block. The textbook guarantee assumes exchangeable data; space breaks it. Spatially aware conformal methods are an open, publishable problem.
- **T6.** On one simulated stand, two published equations [@chave2005tree; @komiyama2005mangrove] differ by about 8 %, while a ±10 % uncertainty in wood density alone spreads each answer by about ±16 %. Wood density, not only the equation, deserves the field effort.

### LiDAR and hazards (T7 to T12)

{{< include _snippets/ch36c_bank_lidar_hazards.qmd >}}

- **T7.** The same 0.81 ha yields 178 trees or 117 depending on one window parameter. Only field stems can set it.
- **T8.** Where ETH reads above 30 m, it is on average 12 m taller than GLAD. Which is right needs local airborne LiDAR.
- **T9.** Thirty plots placed by clustering the embedding space cover the landscapes of West Java better than every one of 300 random designs. Optimising this for real flight costs is the thesis.
- **T10.** Inside one Iburi window a model tested on the other half of the area loses nothing (F1 0.75 both ways). That is the easy test; the hard one is a second earthquake.
- **T11.** The two footprint layers disagree wildly: Google finds about twice Microsoft's buildings in Java's towns, none at all in Kuala Simpang (Aceh), and Microsoft has none in Jayapura. Exposure numbers inherit this.
- **T12.** Averaged amplitude barely separates landslide ground from its surroundings, before or after the earthquake. A warning, if one exists, will come from coherence or texture.

### Methods (T13 to T15)

{{< include _snippets/ch36d_bank_methods.qmd >}}

- **T13.** With map labels near Bandung, random and 5 km block validation agree (0.87 and 0.86). Chapter [-@sec-sampling] found a large gap with field labels. Knowing when spatial validation matters is itself the question.
- **T14.** About 18 % of West Java lies outside the area of applicability of a model trained near Bandung, mostly in the north-east and along the south coast.
- **T15.** Terra and Aqua both show dry-season "cooling" over West Java, at different rates (−0.29 and −0.46 °C per decade). A real surface trend should not depend on the satellite.

## Before you commit to a topic
Search Google Scholar and Scopus for the last two years with the topic's key terms. Read the three most cited and the three most recent papers. Write one paragraph on what they did not do. If you cannot write that paragraph, pick another topic. Area estimates in any thesis should follow good practice for accuracy and area [@olofsson2014good].
:::
